name: Shinekhen Buryat
confidence_why: Yamakoshi 2011 and Yamakoshi 2003, the only first-hand descriptions of Shinekhen Buryat and both drawn from the same 2000-2002 fieldwork, agree that stress falls on the first syllable unless a later syllable has a long vowel or diphthong, while Poppe 1932's fixed: initial syllable stress describes the neighbouring New Barga variety as spoken around 1930 and does not bear on this record.

catalog_quote: 2.2 Suprasegmental phonology. Shinekhen Buryat has two accent systems: pitch accent and stress accent. Both systems are phonologically indistinctive, and clitics are not accentuated. a. Stress accent. The initial syllable is stressed. If VV (long vowel or diphthong) are found in other syllables, the syllable that has VV is stressed. E.g. xórgan 'lamb', teméen 'camel', gasʲóon 'bitter'. b. Pitch accent. V1 of the last syllable are pitched higher. E.g. xorgaꜜn 'lamb', temeꜜen 'camel', jabxa '(someone) will go'. [fn. 2:] 'ꜜ' indicates pitch fall. If the last syllable has neither V2 nor C2 (like jabxa presented above), the pitch does not fall. ... new_statements.quote: [p. 82] シネヘン・ブリヤート語は，他のモンゴル諸語同様，アクセントによる意味の弁別がなく，いわゆる固定アクセントの体系をなしている． [pp. 83-84, sec. 5.2] モンゴル語，ブリヤート語などで言われる強弱アクセントは，弱化母音の現れない位置が相対的に強，さらに非弱化母音のうち，第一音節短母音と第二音節以降の VV とでは VV のほうが相対的に強，と換言できるだろう．シネヘン・ブリヤート語でも同様で，弱化母音は通常，第二音節以降の短母音にあらわれる．また，シネヘン・ブリヤート語では高低アクセントも確認される．規則は (16) の通り．(16) (8) のような音節構造を規定した場合，高低アクセントは原則として最終音節の C1 の直前で上昇し，最終音節 V1 の直後で下降するという形式であらわれる．なお，最終音節が V1 で終わる語の場合は，上昇調のまま下降しない．なお，倚辞的な単位である小詞は，それ自体にアクセントの山を持たない．
new_statements.translation: [p. 82] Shinekhen Buryat, like the other Mongolic languages, has no distinction of meaning by accent and forms a so-called fixed-accent system. [pp. 83-84, sec. 5.2] The 'stress (strong-weak) accent' spoken of for Mongolian, Buryat and so on can be restated as follows: the positions in which reduced vowels do not appear are relatively strong, and further, among the unreduced vowels, between a first-syllable short vowel and a VV (long vowel or diphthong) of the second syllable onward, the VV is relatively stronger. The same holds in Shinekhen Buryat, where reduced vowels normally appear in the short vowels of the second syllable onward. In addition, a pitch accent is also attested in Shinekhen Buryat; the rule is as in (16). (16) Given a syllable structure such as (8), the pitch accent in principle appears in the form of a rise immediately before C1 of the final syllable and a fall immediately after V1 of the final syllable. Note that in words whose final syllable ends in V1 the pitch stays in the rising contour and does not fall. Note also that particles, which are enclitic units, do not have an accent peak of their own.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record from Yamakoshi 2011 (initial syllable by default; a non-initial VV syllable is stressed instead; stress non-distinctive; clitics unaccented; coexisting final-syllable pitch accent with fall after final V1 and no fall when the word ends in V1). Adds: (a) the author's explicit stance that the Mongolic 'stress accent' is relative prominence of unreduced vowels (initial short V and non-initial VV strong, VV the stronger) and that he adopts the pitch accent analysis (position B) as primary; (b) the exact rise/fall loci of the pitch accent (rise before C1 of the final syllable, fall after V1); (c) suffixes shift the pitch peak while enclitic particles do not;…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent is non-distinctive ('fixed accent system'). Stress-type prominence: the first-syllable vowel (never reduced) is relatively strong against reduced non-initial short vowels, and a non-initial long vowel or diphthong (VV) is relatively stronger than the initial short vowel, i.e. default initial, a non-initial heavy (VV) syllable takes the prominence; the author frames this as relative phonetic strength driven by non-initial short-vowel reduction rather than as a categorical stress rule, and in sec. 5.1 (p. 83) says he takes the pitch accent position (B) as his primary description. The pitch accent is fixed on the final syllable: rise immediately before the onset C1 of the final syllable, fall immediately after its V1; no fall when the word ends in V1. Suffixes and inflectional endings are inside the domain and shift the peak (17: adôon, adoon-âi, adoon-dâ, adoo-g-âar); enclitic particles have no peak of their own and do not move the host's peak (18: adôon=sʲe bai-nâ; 19-20).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated for accent; the paper does not say which VV wins when a word has more than one non-initial long vowel or diphthong; it notes (p. 84) that some forms whose status as ending vs. particle is disputed are classed as particles on the phonological criterion that they do not shift the pitch peak, with the ending/particle classification deferred to a later paper
new_statements.identity_note: Yamakoshi 2003 describes Shinekhen Buryat proper: p. 69 footnote * states the data were collected in summers 2000-2002 in Hulunbuir City (呼倫貝爾市, then Hulunbuir League), Inner Mongolia, from named speakers (dogarmaa, 70s, f; dolmaa, 60s, f; mizʲidzʲab, sedenzʲab, dasʲdondog, 30s, m); fn. 1 refers to Yamakoshi 2002a, b for the language overview. This is the eastern (Aga/Khori-type) Buryat emigrant variety, not the New Barga (Bargu) lect that Glottolog names as the dialect of chin1476 'China Buriat'.

sources.citation: Poppe, N. 1932. Skizze der Phonetik des Bargu-Burjätischen. Asia Major (first series) 7(3): 307-378.
sources.quote: 'Der dynamische Akzent, welcher hier nicht bezeichnet wird, da er immer auf der ersten Silbe ruht, ist ebenso wie im Khalkhamongolischen sehr kraeftig ... Ausser dem dynamischen Akzent besitzt das Wort auch einen musikalischen Akzent, welcher auf die letzte Silbe faellt.' I.e. fixed initial dynamic stress (no long-vowel attraction mentioned) plus a final-syllable musical accent. NOTE: this describes New Barga (Sine-Bargu) as recorded c. 1930, not the Shinekhen Buryat (Aga-Buryat emigrant) variety our record codes; Glottolog files it under chin1476 but it is a different lect.

sources.note: The only dedicated phonology paper on Shinekhen Buryat, with a 3-page accent section that frames 'stress' as relative prominence tied to vowel (non-)reduction and treats final-syllable pitch accent as the primary word-prosodic system; useful to annotate the record's caution field.

sources.quote: p. 82: Shinekhen Buryat, like the other Mongolic languages, has no meaning distinctions by accent and forms a so-called fixed-accent system. p. 83 (5.1) reviews the two positions on Mongolian/Buryat accent: A. stress accent, either (a) always on the first syllable (Schmidt 1832, Luvsanvandan et al. 1966) or (b) basically first syllable but moving to a non-initial syllable containing a long vowel or diphthong (Poppe 1951, 1960, Street 1963); B. pitch accent (Hattori 1951, Kakudo 1982).
